sections.h2: Who handles property tax in Terrebonne Parish?
sections.html:
The Terrebonne Parish Assessor values property, and the Terrebonne Parish Sheriff's tax office collects the bill. The Assessor's site lists 985-876-6620 for the office, in the Government Tower in Houma, open Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m.

The same site gives 985-857-0230 for the Tax Collector's office, which handles payment of tax bills. We did not find a street address on the pages we opened, so call before visiting.

sections.h2: How are homes assessed in Terrebonne Parish?
sections.html:
Residential property is assessed at 10% of fair market value, and a statewide reassessment is required at least every four years. The assessed value is then multiplied by the millage rates levied by each taxing body.

One mill is $1 for every $1,000 of assessed value, so a 20-mill tax is $20 per $1,000. A $200,000 house would carry a $20,000 assessed value before any exemption, and the homestead exemption removes $7,500 of that. This is an illustration, not a quote for any house.

We could not confirm a current parish millage on an opened official page, so we do not give one. The Assessor and the Tax Collector can tell you which levies apply to a Houma address versus one on a bayou outside the city.

sections.h2: How do you appeal a Terrebonne Parish assessment?
sections.html:
You review your assessment while the roll is open for inspection, then appeal to the local Board of Review if you disagree. State guidance puts the inspection window between August 15 and September 15 in most parishes.

  • Pull your parcel record and check the facts on it.
  • Collect evidence such as a recent appraisal, damage photos or repair estimates.
  • Contact the Assessor before the Board of Review deadline, which varies by year.

After the Board of Review, the taxpayer can go to the Louisiana Tax Commission and then to court. Storm-damaged houses are the ones where an owner most often has a case to bring, so a Hurricane Ida repair file is useful.

sections.h2: When is Terrebonne Parish property tax due and what if you miss it?
sections.html:
Tax is due December 31, and unpaid tax carries 1% interest per month. The parish tax collector mails bills each December, according to the House Fiscal Division.

If the tax is still unpaid, the collector can sell the property at a tax sale, and the owner of immovable property sold this way has three years to redeem it. Treat that as a safety net, not a plan, because costs and interest keep growing.

When you sell, the unpaid tax is paid from the proceeds at closing. A payoff letter from the Tax Collector at 985-857-0230 gives the title company a number to work from.

sections.h2: How is Terrebonne Parish governed and how does that touch the tax bill?
sections.html:
Terrebonne Parish runs a consolidated government, and Houma's city government was merged into it in 1984. The Terrebonne Parish Consolidated Government provides police and fire protection inside Houma, plus an urban electric system and a parish gas utility, according to the Louisiana Legislative Auditor's financial reports.

Louisiana tax bills combine levies from several taxing bodies. Which ones appear on your bill depends on the address, so a house inside Houma and one on a bayou road can carry different totals.

  • Check the parcel record for the taxing districts listed.
  • Compare last year's bill with this year's assessed value.
  • Ask the Tax Collector about any special districts that apply.

The Terrebonne Parish School District covers the whole parish, and the parish has eight library branches, which is useful context for a buyer comparing areas.

sections.h2: What is Terrebonne Parish like, and how does it affect a sale?
sections.html:
Terrebonne Parish was created on March 22, 1822, and Houma, its seat, has 33,406 residents in the 2020 census. The parish has 109,580 people, down to an estimated 104,163 in 2025, and it covers 1,232 square miles of land and 850 of water.

The economy leans on oil and gas, seafood, shipbuilding, medical services and tourism. The parish is fifth in Louisiana by land area, and Bayou Cane is the largest unincorporated area next to Houma.

Houma gets about 65 inches of rain a year, mostly from June through September, and sits at about 10 feet above sea level. FEMA said new flood maps for the parish would take effect on September 7, 2023, so check where your parcel falls before you list.

Hurricane Ida hit Houma on August 29, 2021 as a Category 4 storm with 150 mph winds at landfall near Port Fourchon, and many houses were damaged or destroyed. Hurricane Francine made landfall in the parish on September 11, 2024.

sections.h2: What places and roads make up Terrebonne Parish?
sections.html:
Houma is the parish seat and largest city, and Wikipedia says it was settled by the Chitimacha and then the Houma people before European colonization. Founding dates for the city differ between 1832 and 1834, and incorporation came in 1848.

Wikipedia lists Bayou Cane, Montegut, Dulac, Chauvin, Dularge, Gibson and Pointe-au-Chien among the parish's communities. The Houma metro area, which also includes the Thibodaux area, had 208,178 people in 2020.

Houma-Terrebonne Airport is about 3 miles southeast of the downtown area, and Good Earth Transit runs five major bus routes, including service to Thibodaux. Most residents rely on cars. The Intracoastal Waterway and the Houma Navigational Canal remain part of local commerce.

Vietnamese refugee families settled in the area in the 1970s, and many still work in shrimping, which is one of several ways the fishing economy shows up in local property types, from bayou camps to older homes near docks.

sections.h2: What should you gather before selling a Terrebonne house with tax due?
sections.html:
Gather a tax payoff, the parcel record, your deed and any storm repair papers. Together they let a buyer or title company move quickly.

Assessment and parcel recordAssessor, 985-876-6620
Recorded deed and mortgage historyTerrebonne Parish Clerk of Court
Flood zone statusCurrent FEMA flood map for the parish

If you are behind on tax and the house is also in poor repair, say so up front. A buyer who knows the full picture can set a price and a timeline that account for it.

sections.h2: How do sellers handle tax and storm damage together?
sections.html:
Sellers in Terrebonne Parish often have both a tax bill and a house that has seen storm damage, and a cash sale as-is can address both at once. The buyer takes the repairs, and the title company pays the tax from the proceeds.

  • Get your tax payoff in writing.
  • Collect roof and repair records from Ida or Francine.
  • Check flood zone status on the current FEMA map.
  • Record the sale with the Terrebonne Clerk of Court after closing.

The deed must name who is responsible for property taxes, so the buyer's bill goes to the right address next December.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Terrebonne Parish?
faqs.a: The Terrebonne Parish Sheriff's tax office collects it. The Tax Collector's phone listed on the Assessor's site is 985-857-0230.

faqs.q: When is Terrebonne Parish property tax due?
faqs.a: It is due December 31 under state rules, and interest of 1% per month applies afterward.

faqs.q: What is the homestead exemption in Terrebonne Parish?
faqs.a: It removes $7,500 of assessed value, which equals $75,000 of fair market value, for an owner-occupied home.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my Terrebonne Parish assessment?
faqs.a: Review it during the roll inspection period and then appeal to the Board of Review. The inspection window is usually August 15 to September 15.

faqs.q: Can I sell a hurricane-damaged house in Terrebonne Parish?
faqs.a: Yes. Houses can be sold as-is, and any unpaid tax is settled from the proceeds at closing.
